title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: "the moon was born from his mind." the Purusha Sukta turns the parts of a body into the sky, the wind and the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's hardest verse: mouth, arms, thighs and feet as four groups, and the honest argument over what that means.

The moon was born from his mind. That's a line from the Purusha Sukta, in paraphrase, and it comes with a whole list. The sun, from his eye. The wind, from his breath. The sky, from his head. Look up some clear night and try reading the sky that way: not as a ceiling, but as a face, a breath, a mind, far bigger than yours and somehow related to yours. The hymn has turned from the people of the world to the world itself, and it draws the map with a body.
screen: `THE MOON, FROM HIS MIND.` → `THE SUN, FROM HIS EYE.` → `A SKY MADE FROM A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen, in Sanskrit, begins chandrama manaso jatah: the moon, born from mind. From his eye, the sun. From his mouth, Indra and Agni, the god of storm and the god of fire. From his breath, Vayu, the wind. Verse fourteen goes on. From his navel, the middle air. From his head, the sky took shape. From his feet, the earth. From his ear, the directions. And so, it says, they fashioned the worlds. Listen to how the pairs fit. Eye and sun: light and seeing. Breath and wind: the same moving air, small and large. Feet and earth: what stands, and what is stood on. Ear and the directions: sound comes from every side. Mind and moon is harder. Some readers hear the moon's waxing and waning as a mind that changes, but the verse only sets the two side by side. Earlier on this path, the Aitareya Upanishad told the same story in reverse: fire became speech and entered the mouth, wind became breath and entered the nose, the sun became sight and entered the eyes, the moon became mind. Together they make a loop. The world comes out of a person, and the world's powers come back to live in a person. This week ran from the Nasadiya's cord and open ending into the Purusha: a thousand heads, the quarter we can see, the great offering, the hard verse, and now the sky. One person, and everything.
screen: `MIND TO MOON, EYE TO SUN.` · `BREATH TO WIND, FEET TO EARTH.` · `THE AITAREYA: THE SAME, IN REVERSE.` · `ONE PERSON, AND EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Feel the breath at the nostrils and let it be wind for a moment; notice light through closed eyelids and let it be the sun; feel the feet on the floor and let it be the earth; listen for sounds from every side. Then rest the mind and let it be as quiet as the moon, going slowly, body, then world, then body again; if you pray, you can pray there.
The Purusha Sukta. In verses thirteen and fourteen, mind becomes the moon, eye the sun, breath the wind, feet the earth, and so the worlds are fashioned.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. The moon from his mind, the sun from his eye. A week on the hill, done.

howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting, and its picture of the world fashioned from the cosmic person's body is echoed in later texts such as the Aitareya Upanishad.
